passages.t: Jerusalem besieged, and the temple vessels carried off
passages.happening:
The book opens with a date and a disaster. ‘In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it’ (verse 1).

The next verse says who was really at work. ‘And the Lord delivered into his hand Jehoiakim king of Judah, along with some of the articles from the house of God’ (verse 2). Nebuchadnezzar carried the sacred vessels to the land of Shinar and put them in the treasury of his god.
passages.hearers:
Jehoiakim ruled Judah from about 609 to 598 BC. In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar, then crown prince, defeated the Egyptian army at Carchemish on the Euphrates and moved south. That same year his father died and he became king. Jehoiakim, who had been Egypt's vassal, now submitted to Babylon. A small number of hostages from leading families were taken then. A larger deportation followed in 597 BC, and Jerusalem was destroyed in 587 or 586 BC.

The first hearers would have caught the weight of verse 2. Babylon's victory was not the defeat of Israel's God. The Lord delivered the king into Nebuchadnezzar's hand. The book begins by saying that God is still in charge, even of the exile.

Taking a temple's vessels as trophies and placing them in the treasury of the victor's god was a claim that the god of the conquered had lost. The god here is probably Marduk, the patron god of Babylon. And the land is called Shinar, an old name for Babylonia that recalls the tower of Babel. The first hearers would have heard the echo: the old city of human pride.
passages.later: The vessels come back into the story twice. Belshazzar drinks from them at his feast (Daniel 5:2-3), and later King Cyrus ‘brought out the articles belonging to the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem’ (Ezra 1:7) and sent them home. The Chronicler tells the same taking: ‘Nebuchadnezzar also took to Babylon some of the articles from the house of the LORD’ (2 Chronicles 36:7).
passages.hard:
Does the date in verse 1 conflict with Jeremiah and with Babylonian records?

Daniel puts the siege in Jehoiakim's third year, while Jeremiah equates Jehoiakim's fourth year with Nebuchadnezzar's first (Jeremiah 25:1). Many explain the difference by two ways of counting reigns. Babylon treated the part-year in which a king took the throne as his accession year and began counting from the next new year, while Judah often counted that part-year as year one. On that reckoning Daniel's third year and Jeremiah's fourth can be the same year, 605 BC.

A second question is that the Babylonian Chronicle, which records Nebuchadnezzar's campaigns, does not mention a siege of Jerusalem in 605 BC, though it records his conquest of the region that year. Those who hold a sixth-century date note that the chronicle is brief and that 2 Kings 24:1 confirms Jehoiakim became his vassal. Many critical scholars think the author compressed or combined events. Either way, the verse's point stands: God handed Judah over.
passages.asks: The book opens by saying that even the exile was in God's hands. Ask where you find it hardest to believe that God is still at work in a loss. And ask what holy things in your own life have been carried off into the service of something else.

passages.t: Young nobles chosen, trained and renamed
passages.happening:
The king orders Ashpenaz, the chief of his court officials, to bring in young men from Israel's royal family and nobility (verse 3). They are to be without blemish, handsome, gifted and quick to learn, fit to serve in the palace, and the court will ‘teach them the language and literature of the Chaldeans’ (verse 4).

They are given daily food and wine from the king's table, and they are to be trained for three years before entering his service (verse 5). Among them are four from Judah: Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah (verse 6).

The chief official gives them new names. Daniel becomes Belteshazzar, Hananiah becomes Shadrach, Mishael becomes Meshach, and Azariah becomes Abednego (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Taking the sons of conquered royalty and nobility to be raised at court was common imperial practice. It kept their families at home loyal, and it produced officials who could serve the empire in its provinces.

The Chaldeans were the people whose dynasty ruled Babylon, and in Daniel the word also names a class of scholars and diviners. Their learning was vast and written on clay: Akkadian and Sumerian texts, mathematics, astronomy, and great collections of omens for reading the will of the gods from dreams, stars and the organs of sacrificed animals. Daniel and his friends were trained in all of it. The book does not treat learning Babylon's wisdom as sin.

The renaming was a claim of ownership. Each Hebrew name honored Israel's God. Daniel speaks of God as judge, Hananiah means the LORD has been gracious, Mishael who is what God is, and Azariah the LORD has helped. Belteshazzar is a Babylonian name that probably asks a god to protect the king's life. Abednego means servant of Nego, which many think is an altered form of Nabu, a Babylonian god. The empire was renaming them for its own gods.

The word for court official, saris, is sometimes translated eunuch. Whether these young men were made eunuchs is uncertain.
passages.later: The prophet Isaiah had warned King Hezekiah that ‘some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon’ (Isaiah 39:7), and some interpreters connect that warning with this chapter. Jeremiah later wrote to the exiles, ‘Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles’ (Jeremiah 29:7).
passages.asks: Daniel and his friends were given new names, a new language and a new education, and they took them. Ask which parts of the culture around you a believer can learn and use, and which parts would claim ownership of you. And ask what names the world around you tries to give you.

passages.t: Daniel's resolve and the ten-day test
passages.happening:
‘But Daniel made up his mind that he would not defile himself with the king’s food or wine’ (verse 8). So he asks the chief official for permission.

God had given Daniel favor and compassion with the official (verse 9), but the official is afraid. If the king sees these young men looking thinner than the others, it will cost the official his head (verse 10).

So Daniel goes to the steward over the four and proposes a test. ‘Please test your servants for ten days’ (verse 12). Give them only vegetables and water, then compare them with the young men who eat the royal food (verses 12-13). The steward agrees.

‘And at the end of ten days, they looked healthier and better nourished than all the young men who were eating the king’s food’ (verse 15). So the steward keeps giving them vegetables instead of the king's food and wine (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The verb for defile, ga'al, describes something made unfit for worship or use before God. Daniel's concern is not diet as such. It is defilement: he will not let the king's table compromise his standing before God.

Why he refused is debated. Royal meat would not have followed the food laws of Leviticus, and both meat and wine may have been offered to idols first. Others suggest that eating from the king's table bound a person in loyalty to the king, so that plain food kept the young men visibly dependent on God. The text does not settle the reason.

What it does show is the manner of the refusal. Daniel draws a line without rebellion. He asks permission. He understands the official's fear and offers a way that protects him. He proposes a test with a clear time and a clear result. The verb for test, nasah, is the one used when God tests Abraham. Here Daniel proposes the test himself, trusting God to honor faithfulness in a way the official can see.

Notice too who acts first in verse 9. God had granted Daniel favor. The courage is Daniel's, and the open door is God's.
passages.later: The law Daniel kept told Israel to ‘distinguish between the unclean and the clean, between animals that may be eaten and those that may not’ (Leviticus 11:47). Long before, another young Hebrew in a foreign court had been given favor with his master: Joseph, of whom Pharaoh said ‘there is no one as discerning and wise as you’ (Genesis 41:39).
passages.hard:
Why did Daniel refuse the food, and is this chapter a rule about diet?

The chapter gives no reason beyond defilement, and readers have proposed three: the food laws, food offered to idols, and the loyalty that the king's table implied. Each has its supporters, and the text does not decide.

It is not a diet plan. The young men's health after ten days is a sign that God honored their faithfulness, not a claim that vegetables are better than meat.

The lesson the chapter teaches is about where to draw a line, and how. A faithful person may serve in a foreign court, learn its learning and answer to its name, and still keep a boundary that belongs to God alone, held with courtesy and courage.
passages.asks: Daniel made up his mind before the test came. Ask where you have decided in advance what you will not do, and where you are still deciding under pressure. And ask how you can hold a line of conscience without contempt for the people around you.

passages.t: God gives wisdom, and the four enter the king's service
passages.happening:
‘To these four young men God gave knowledge and understanding in every kind of literature and wisdom’ (verse 17). And Daniel had insight into all kinds of visions and dreams.

At the end of the three years the chief official presents them to Nebuchadnezzar. The king speaks with them and finds no one equal to them, so they enter his service (verses 18-19). In every matter he consults them about, ‘he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his entire kingdom’ (verse 20).

‘And Daniel remained there until the first year of King Cyrus’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Three times in this chapter the Hebrew verb natan, to give, has God as its subject. God gave Jehoiakim into Nebuchadnezzar's hand (verse 2). God gave Daniel favor (verse 9). God gave the four knowledge and wisdom (verse 17). The first hearers were being shown who is really in charge of the story.

The ten days of testing are echoed by the result. After three years the king finds the four ten times better than his experts. Daniel's gift for dreams and visions is mentioned here at the start, because the next chapter will need it.

The last verse spans the whole exile in a sentence. Daniel remained until the first year of Cyrus, the Persian king who took Babylon in 539 BC and let the exiles go home. The first hearers would have heard the quiet promise in it. Babylon would not last, and Daniel would outlive it.
passages.later: The same pattern appears in Joseph's story, where Pharaoh asks, ‘Can we find anyone like this man, in whom the Spirit of God abides?’ (Genesis 41:38). And the end of Babylon that verse 21 foreshadows is told in Daniel 5, where the kingdom is ‘given over to the Medes and Persians’ (Daniel 5:28).
passages.asks: The chapter says three times that God gave. Ask what in your own work and gifts has been given to you rather than earned. And ask how you would serve differently if you believed, as verse 21 hints, that the powers around you will not last.
